partial:
partial Settled #

Upper bounds — holds for every partial

  • \(\mathrm{C}^0(f) \le \mathrm{C}(f)\)
    The mirror of the $\mathrm{C}^1$ line above: a maximum over the $0$-inputs is a maximum over a subset of the domain. Recorded at partial rather than relation only because $\mathrm{C}^0$ needs a distinguished "no" answer to mean anything, so the relational cell is not the zoo's to fill; the bound still travels up to total on its own.

Tight, and by the dullest possible witness: a $0$-input of $\mathrm{OR}_n$ is the all-zero string and certifying it takes all $n$ bits, so $\mathrm{C}^0(\mathrm{OR}_n) = \mathrm{C}(\mathrm{OR}_n) = n$.

Trivial, and the reason it is worth writing down: without it the whole $\mathrm{C}^0$ row has no upper bound of any kind, because the one recorded $\mathrm{C}^0$ bound -- $\mathrm{C}^0 \le \mathrm{s}^1\,\mathrm{bs}^0$ [Nisan91] -- is a product of two measures and so carries no exponent. With this line the row inherits everything $\mathrm{C}$ has: $\mathrm{C}^0 \le \mathrm{C} \le \mathrm{D}$, $\mathrm{C}^0 \le \mathrm{R}_0$, $\mathrm{C}^0 = O(\mathrm{R}^2)$, and so on.

Note what does not follow. $\mathrm{D} \le \mathrm{C}^0\mathrm{C}^1$ [Tardos89] needs both sides: $\mathrm{D}$ is not bounded by $\mathrm{C}^0$ alone, since $\mathrm{C}^0(\mathrm{AND}_n) = 1$ while $\mathrm{D} = n$. The $\mathrm{C}^0$ column stays empty for that reason, and legitimately.

see also: \(\mathrm{C}^0(f)\), \(\mathrm{C}(f)\), \(\mathrm{C}^1(f)\), \(\mathrm{D}(f)\), \(\mathrm{OR}_n\), \(\mathrm{AND}_n\) data/relations/13-definitional.yaml

total:
total No bound exists #

Upper bounds — holds for every total

  • \(\mathrm{C}^0(f) \le \mathrm{s}^1(f)\,\mathrm{bs}^0(f)\)
    Nisan91 BdW02
    Nisan's argument, kept one-sided: take a maximal family of disjoint minimal sensitive blocks at a $0$-input $x$; each has size at most $\mathrm{s}^1(f)$ because flipping it lands on a $1$-input all of whose bits in the block are sensitive. Their union is a $0$-certificate. No form: -- the bound is a product of two other measures, and the $\mathrm{s}^1$ factor is not decoration: it is the whole content of the bound.
  • \(\mathrm{C}^0(f) \le \mathrm{s}(f)\,\mathrm{bs}^0(f) \le \mathrm{bs}(f)\,\mathrm{bs}^0(f)\)
    Nisan91

Lower bounds / separations — there is a family achieving this

  • \(\mathrm{bs}^0(f) \le \mathrm{C}^0(f)\)
    Disjoint sensitive blocks must each be touched by any certificate.
  • \(\mathrm{C}^0(g_n) = \Theta(n),\quad \mathrm{bs}^0(g_n) = O(1)\)
    witness: \(g_n\) GSS16
    The \(g_n\) gadget: the indicator of $2^{n/50}$ random points. They are far apart, so a $0$-input has $O(1)$ disjoint sensitive blocks; they are dense, so no subcube of codimension $n/100$ misses them and every $0$-certificate is linear.

There is no upper bound on $\mathrm{C}^0$ in terms of $\mathrm{bs}^0$ alone, of any shape. Both recorded inequalities are products, and the witness shows the second factor is doing all the work: at $g_n$ the bound reads $n \le n\cdot O(1)$.

This is the one-sided anomaly. Two-sidedly $\mathrm{C}\le\mathrm{s}\cdot \mathrm{bs}\le\mathrm{bs}^2$ and the exponent $2$ is attained (\(f_{\mathrm{GSS}}\)), so $\mathrm{C}$ vs $\mathrm{bs}$ is settled; but the $0$-side of $\mathrm{C}$ is controlled by the $1$-side of $\mathrm{s}$, and a function whose $1$-side is maximally sensitive can hide an arbitrarily large $0$-certificate behind a constant $\mathrm{bs}^0$. Composing with $\mathrm{OR}_n$ trades the unbounded ratio for the quadratic one: it multiplies $\mathrm{bs}^0$ by $n$ and $\mathrm{C}^0$ by $n$ as well, turning $g_n$ into a family where both sides are polynomial and the exponent $2$ can be read off.

A hypothesis that does buy the bound: for monotone $f$ the three measures collapse pointwise, $\mathrm{s}(f,x)=\mathrm{C}(f,x)$ for every $x$ [Nisan91], so $\mathrm{s}^0=\mathrm{bs}^0=\mathrm{C}^0$ exactly and the cell is settled at exponent $1$. The witness is as far from monotone as a function gets -- an indicator of scattered points.

see also: \(\mathrm{C}^0(f)\), \(\mathrm{bs}^0(f)\), \(\mathrm{s}^1(f)\), \(\mathrm{bs}(f)\), \(\mathrm{C}(f)\), \(g_n\), \(f_{\mathrm{GSS}}\) data/relations/10-new-measures.yaml
